pages.text: Sociology Standards Sociology Standards Skip Navigation Sociology Standards The U.S. Census Bureau’s Statistics in Schools (SIS) activities are based on relevant education standards and guidelines that outline the foundational knowledge and skills students should have at certain levels. The SIS activities — which are designed to supplement or guide, not replace, existing curricula — help develop these skills and knowledge. Not all educators use the same standards. These standards are organized by four learning domains; each represents a broad area of sociological knowledge and study appropriate for high school. Stefanie Koperniak | MIT Open Learning With war continuing to disrupt education for millions of Ukrainian high school and college students, many are turning to online resources, including MIT OpenCourseWare, a part of MIT Open Learning offering educational materials from more than 2,500 MIT undergraduate and graduate courses. For Ukrainian high school senior Sofiia Lipkevych and other students, MIT OpenCourseWare has provided valuable opportunities to take courses in key subject areas. However, while multiple Ukrainian students study English, many do not yet have sufficient command of the language to be able to fully understand and use the often very technical and complex OpenCourseWare content and materials. “At my school, I saw firsthand how language barriers prevented many Ukrainian students from accessing world-class education,” says Lipkevych. She was able to address this challenge as a participant in the Ukrainian Leadership and Technology Academy (ULTA), established by Ukrainian MIT students Dima Yanovsky and Andrii Zahorodnii. Soil & Groundwater Remediation During a Groundwater University site tour at the Santa Susana Field Laboratory, Josh Mengers, federal project director for the Energy Technology Engineering Center, shows an educational model to demonstrate some of the work being done at the site. The Department of Energy’s (DOE) Office of Environmental Management (EM) manages one of the largest groundwater and soil remediation efforts in the world. The inventory at the EM sites includes 6.5 trillion liters of contaminated groundwater, an amount equal to about four times the daily U.S. water consumption, and 40 million cubic meters of soil and debris contaminated with radionuclides, metals, and organics. EM’s Office of Subsurface Closure is working with EM site managers around the country to help find solutions to their specific technical issues. At the large sites such as Hanford, Savannah River and Oak Ridge, the Office of Subsurface Closure has conducted research and demonstration projects to test new technologies and remediation approaches. The primary goal of the Office of Subsurface Closure is to expedite closure of major soil and groundwater sites and waste units. By Lauren Rebecca Thacker As an undergraduate considering her future career, Sok Danica, a recent graduate of National University of Management in Phnom Penh, Cambodia, sought advice from professors and lecturers. One lecturer, who also worked as a financial analyst, suggested MIT Open Learning as a way to explore her interests and find out which subjects sparked passion and curiosity. Sok, who majored in global entrepreneurship and innovations, decided to check out Principles of Microeconomics , taught by Jonathan Gruber and published by Open Learning’s MIT OpenCourseWare. She had some background knowledge of finance but felt intimidated by the course. “I thought, ‘This is MIT and my IQ isn’t where those geniuses are,’ she remembers. “But Professor Gruber never did anything to make anyone feel like they didn’t belong. Solar Energy The sun emits solar radiation in the form of light. Solar energy technologies capture this radiation and turn it into useful forms of energy. There are two main types of solar energy technologies—photovoltaics (PV) and concentrating solar-thermal power (CSP). Why Go Solar? Millions of Americans are deciding to power their homes with solar energy—especially as costs have decreased—but an investment in solar energy generates more than just clean energy. It can support household savings, energy independence, economic opportunities, grid reliability, resilience, security and affordability, and a safer planet. Solar energy creates household savings. Solar owners can reduce their energy bills with savings that will accrue for the lifetime of the system. Community solar can provide savings for those who rent their homes or whose roofs aren’t suitable for solar panels. Solar deployment generates economic opportunities. But the monument has more to offer, including distinctive mountains rising from the desert floor. It has three distinct mountain ranges: the Maricopa, Sand Tank, and Table Top mountains, as well as the Booth and White hills, all separated by wide valleys. You can hike or ride horseback almost everywhere in the monument. Four designated trails in three congressionally designated wilderness areas total 26 miles. Many miles of roads are available for mountain biking and motorized vehicle tours. The monument has significant archaeological and historic sites, and remnants of several important historic trails, including the Juan Bautista de Anza and Butterfield Overland national historic trails. The campground has 42 camp sites, including 4 accessible and 2 walk-in sites. All campsites are available on a first-come, first-served basis. The campground is equipped with restrooms, water, picnic tables, and fire rings. Campers may also enjoy a short hike along the Sourdough Creek Interpretive Trail within the campground. The boat launch area is the take-out for float trips on the Gulkana Wild and Scenic River and provides river access to both motorized boaters and floaters. Recreation In addition to RV and tent recreational camping opportunities, the campground provides access to the Gulkana Wild and Scenic River. Floaters use the boat launch as a put-in and take-out point as well as jet boat users in the river corridor. Activities this site supports include recreational fishing from the bank, subsistence hunting access for caribou and moose, as well as berry picking and trapping. pages.text: South Korea 2026: When to visit, where to stay, and what to do | National Geographic National Geographic Traveller (UK) content straight to your inbox — sign up for our newsletter here TRAVEL BEST OF THE WORLD South Korea has never been more popular—here's why you should visit in 2026 From South Korea’s unique culture and customs to its mind-blowing modern innovations—and its first long-distance hiking route—learn how to experience the richness of this extraordinary place. Maltijae Pass is a long, winding road in Boeun-gun, North Chungcheong Province, South Korea. Photograph by Jun Michael Park, National Geographic By Martin Zatko Published October 21, 2025 There’s no doubt about it— South Korea is one of the world’s “it” destinations. The country’s new-found mega-popularity has found itself propelled by the music, films, and drama series of the “ Korean Wave ,” whose ripples only seem to increase in size every year. Even before visiting, many also find themselves addicted to Korea’s famously spicy cuisine, with dishes such as bibimbap and japchae —as well as side-dishes like kimchi , and alcoholic drinks such as soju and makgeolli —becoming increasingly popular worldwide. While Seoul and Busan are as modern as cities come, Korea is also a proudly traditional land, with unique culture and customs resulting from its two-millennium-long chain of unbroken dynastic rule. What was once known as the “Hermit Kingdom” has now well and truly crawled out of its shell, but the country remains sprinkled with Buddhist temples and hermitages, especially around its pine-covered mountains.

The 34-year-old scored 397.5 out of 400 points in the first round, getting just one of 160 questions wrong, which initially raised suspicions and sparked online speculation. Space Exploration and The Universe To build a complete picture of our universe, scientists gather information both in space and on Earth. Many of NASA’s tools that explore deep space rely on radioisotope power systems supported by the Department of Energy (DOE). DOE researchers also contribute to experiments conducted in space. On Earth, researchers use tools like supercomputers, particle detectors, and observatories to answer a variety of questions about our universe, including how the universe evolved, why it is expanding ever faster, and why there is matter at all. DOE’s Contribution to Understanding Our Universe The DOE and its predecessors have long supported NASA missions to space. DOE maintains the infrastructure to develop, manufacture, test, analyze, and deliver radioisotope power systems for space exploration and national security missions. These systems can produce heat and electricity under the harsh conditions in deep space for decades. NASA has used them for missions to study the moon and all of the planets in the solar system except for Mercury. Now, at the end of 2026, Fisher and baseball fans across New England know exactly what the phrase means. The New Hampshire Space Potatoes have become a beloved alternate identity, adopted by the Fisher Cats for a total of nine home games over the past two seasons. In 1719, on land in the current-day New Hampshire town of Derry, Scots-Irish settlers planted the first white potatoes grown in North America. Starship, the world’s largest rocket, standing at 407ft, is expected to orbit Earth about 14 times over the course of 22 hours, before the company catches the rocket at its launchpad at Starbase in south Texas . As smoke plumes wafted from the launch site, SpaceX employees erupted into cheers. pages.text: SpaceX’s Starship returns to launch pad from orbit in victory for company | SpaceX | The Guardian Skip to main content Skip to navigation 1:17 SpaceX’s Starship returns to launch pad from orbit – video SpaceX SpaceX’s Starship returns to launch pad from orbit in victory for company Although booster exploded, company caught upper stage for first time in campaign to make megarocket reusable Uwa Ede-Osifo Sat 14 Nov 2026 17.35 EST Last modified on Tue 17 Nov 2026 12.40 EST Share Prefer the Guardian on Google SpaceX ’s megarocket Starship returned to its Texas launch tower on Saturday, a milestone in the company’s efforts to make the craft suitable for human spaceflight. The 171ft (52-meter) bullet-shaped upper stage descended into the clutch of the tower’s mechanical arms, ending a 22-hour mission where the craft orbited Earth 14 times. Starship’s 15th test flight was envisioned as a historic double-catch mission, where all parts of the rocket would be returned intact to the launch site, rather than recovered from the ocean as with some previous test flights. The hulking spacecraft is comprised of two parts: a lower booster stage called Super Heavy, whose Raptor engines powered the orbital ascent, and an upper stage also called Starship. Those double-catch ambitions were dashed on Friday, when the booster diverted a few minutes after takeoff and exploded in the Gulf of Mexico. pages.text: Spain 2-3 England: How did Thomas Tuchel's side win and what was learned from Argentina defeat? - BBC Sport Image source, Getty Images Image caption, James Trafford (right) kept Spain out in the latter stages By Emlyn Begley BBC Sport journalist Published 16 November 2026 England held on to beat Spain 3-2 with a backs-to-the-wall finale in the Nations League to finish top of their group. But many observers would have been feeling a sense of deja vu from the World Cup semi-final when England sat back and were beaten by Argentina . So what was different this time? BBC Sport has a look. Were the situations the same? First of all the context of the two games was entirely different. England were 1-0 up against Argentina in the 55th minute on neutral territory in Atlanta - and still had all their players. Anthony Gordon had put them ahead but Lionel Messi set up Enzo Fernandez and then Lautaro Martinez late on. But against Spain the best performance of Thomas Tuchel's reign had them 3-0 up through goals from Harry Kane, Ezri Konsa and Ben White. Elliot Anderson then fouled Lamine Yamal for a penalty, which Mikel Oyarzabal scored - and that began the siege at a partisan Riyadh Air Metropolitano. Nico Williams made it 3-2 but Spain could not find an equaliser, thanks in part to England keeper James Trafford. "Half an hour feels like two hours against a team like this [with 10 men]," Tuchel told ITV afterwards. "That's the way it is. In a media theatre at the Metropolitano in Madrid, head coach Tuchel's sixth sense led him to go public with what he was convinced England would produce against the world champions. Tuchel looked his inquisitors in the eyes and declared: "We are up for something spectacular." To say Tuchel and England kept their word was a masterpiece of understatement after the finest night of the head coach's reign resulted in a 3-2 victory that was large parts magnificent, some parts madness - and all parts spectacular. It also ended Spain's 43-game unbeaten run - setting aside their penalty shootout defeat by Portugal in the 2025 Nations League final. pages.description: As Spain prepare to host England in the Nations League, BBC Sport columnist Guillem Balague charts the rise of Unai Simon to become the world's best keeper.
pages.text: Spain v England: How Unai Simon became world's best goalkeeper - BBC Sport By Guillem Balague BBC Sport columnist Published 15 November 2026 Peter Schmeichel handed Unai Simon the Yashin Trophy and the room applauded warmly. Then the world's best goalkeeper spent his time talking about everybody else. Simon thanked his parents and his brother. He thanked his girlfriend for being an "oasis of tranquillity", and the friends from home who remind him that "many of us in this room are privileged". 'La cuadrilla', the gang of lifelong friends that is a traditional part of Basque culture, has a WhatsApp group of its own, and he takes them on holiday every summer. He thanked his coaches and team-mates. Like Simon, none of them are regulars on the covers of the media. Then he talked about a man who could not be in the room at last month's Ballon d'Or ceremony in London, but whose influence lives on - Simon's youth academy mentor Koldo Asua, who died in 2021. The Spain and Athletic Club number one is not your archetypal superstar. In fact, he is the complete opposite. He stays away from the headlines and is relatively low profile when compared with some of the game's other goalkeepers. His position as Spain's number is regularly questioned - as was the decision to name him as the world's best. In the part-beauty pageant election that is the Ballon d'Or, being low key can work against you, but the case on the pitch is easy to state - even though it rattles those who see the Premier League as the highest standard reachable. pages.text: Spain's rail authorities face European fraud probe after Urda rail disaster Skip to content Site search Home News Sport Business Technology Health Culture Arts Travel Earth Audio Video Live Documentaries Weather Newsletters Watch Live Spain's rail authorities face European fraud probe after Urda rail disaster 6 November 2026 Share Save Add as preferred on Google Alba Morgade EPA Last month's train crash in which 69 people died was the second deadly accident on the same high-speed line this year European Union prosecutors have begun investigating the possible misuse of EU funds meant for upgrading the Spanish railway line where a train crash killed 69 people last week. Prosecutors backed by a special unit of Spain's Guardia Civil security force said they were conducting the inquiry at the offices of Adif rail infrastructure authority and rail safety agency AESF. The 28 October accident on the Madrid-Seville high-speed line was one of the worst railway disasters in Europe this century. It is the second EU fraud inquiry opened into Spain's railways this year, after 46 people were killed on the same line at Adamuz in January. Last week, a train operated by state-owned operator Renfe ploughed into the back of a stationary train belonging to private Spanish company Iryo outside the village of Urda, around 130km (80 miles) south of Madrid. The LZB communication system that monitors the position of trains had gone down, and the Renfe train had been given the all clear to start running at normal speed, even though the Iryo train ahead of it had been unable to restart.
